Where it began

Shane Warne was born in Upper Ferntree Gully, on the edge of Melbourne, on 13 September 1969. As a teenager he also played Australian rules football, turning out for St Kilda's under-19s, before cricket claimed him for good, and the ball stayed in his hand rather than at his feet.

He spent a season in Bristol in 1989, sleeping in the attic of the club pavilion, and another as the professional at Accrington. Back at the Australian Cricket Academy, the former Test spinner Terry Jenner helped turn a gifted young bowler into a serious one.

The player

He made his Test debut against India at Sydney in January 1992, and the start was slow. Then, at Old Trafford in 1993, his first ball in an Ashes Test drifted, pitched well outside leg and turned to hit the top of Mike Gatting's off stump. It became known as the Ball of the Century, and the world paid attention.

Over the next 15 years he played 145 Tests and took 708 wickets at 25.42, second only to one other bowler in Test history. He took five in an innings 37 times, ten in a match ten times, and in 2005 he became the first man to reach 600 Test wickets. He was part of the side that won the 1999 World Cup, named man of the match in both the semi-final and the final.

What made him special

Warne could spin the ball a long way on pitches that offered him nothing, and he did it with accuracy and a bag of variations, the flipper chief among them. Above all he had a sense of theatre, and with him bowling every over felt like an event.

He was a fine slip fielder and a useful batsman, with 3,154 Test runs and 12 fifties. The one thing missing is a Test hundred. He was out for 99 at Perth to a ball later shown to be a no-ball, which seems a little unfair on a man who spent his career fooling batsmen.

Away from the middle

After Tests he captained Rajasthan Royals to the first IPL title in 2008 and became a familiar voice in the commentary box. He worked with Muttiah Muralitharan to help Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami, and his foundation gave money to rebuild the ground at Galle. A keen golfer, he once made a hole in one at Augusta.

He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and was made an Officer of the Order of Australia, for what he gave the game. To most of the cricket world he was simply Warnie. He died in 2022, aged 52.

And finally

In his penultimate Test, at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, his home crowd watched him bowl Andrew Strauss for his 700th wicket. A crowd of 89,155 stood to applaud. Plenty of them had grown up being told that leg-spin was a dying art. He had spent 15 years politely proving otherwise.
